title: eight coercion spellings whose member reads a capability are subtracted by one Layer.succeed for that capability, and the program compiles and runs
notes: specification/requirements.mdx, 'Satisfaction': 'Providing a layer to a computation MUST remove matching capabilities from the computation's unsatisfied requirement row. The provider library MUST establish the runtime scope in which `Capability.context()` resolves those instances.' This is the acceptance direction of the coercion family, and it carries a promise the refusal cases cannot: that the row a coercion charges is a REAL row that a layer subtracts and that the member really runs inside the provided scope. A refusal case proves only that something was refused. WHY THE OUTPUT IS THE EVIDENCE AND NOT A FORMALITY: `read()` returns `DBX`, whose length is 3, so every `3` printed here is a capability that was resolved at run time by the layer this case installs. A backend that recorded the row but never lowered the member's access would compile and then panic, and only the printed value distinguishes 'charged' from 'charged and resolvable'. What this case CANNOT see, and it is important that a reader knows it, is a backend that recorded NO row: the layer is installed at run time whether or not a row was inferred, so such a backend prints exactly these eight lines. That blind spot is the entire reason `a-coercion-row-is-not-subtracted-by-the-wrong-layer` exists beside this case, and neither of the two is sufficient alone. The eight spellings are the ones a companion refusal case proves are charged — an arrow property, a function-expression property, a property holding a reference to a function declaration, a shorthand property, a class arrow field, a computed member name, and `Number`/`String` with a PARENTHESISED callee — so the two cases together say the same eight spellings are charged and satisfiable, which is the statement the language actually makes. WHAT THIS CASE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN: the row by inspection. No corpus expectation can read a row; what it can observe is that one `Layer.succeed(Db, db)` subtracts all eight, which is the observable form of the same claim. It also does not use `+obj` anywhere, though the refusal cases do: unary plus on an object type is rejected by stock TypeScript, and an `output` case must survive a stock check of the EMITTED module set, so the number-hint positions here are written as `Number(obj)`. That is a harness constraint and not a language one, and it is recorded here so a future reader does not conclude that `+` is unavailable. WHY THE PRINTED LINES ARE NOT ALL THE SAME: three of them are `DBX` or `1` rather than `3`, so a lowering that reordered, dropped or duplicated a line produces something visibly different rather than a permutation of eight identical strings. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the sixth declared stdout line from `1` to `2` — the computed-member-name line, whose value comes from a different mechanism than the other seven — turns the case red on BOTH backends with the stdout diff printed, and the expectation was restored byte-identically (sha256 b4a1db3b5d4440d2379253bef78766ce0f205e421fb98d0a96f5c44c1f05dd47 before and after, that digest being this file's content at the moment the mutation ran — the sentence recording it is appended afterwards, so the shipped file necessarily hashes differently). Its direct refusal sibling is `a-coercion-row-is-not-subtracted-by-the-wrong-layer`, which provides a DIFFERENT capability to the same shape and must be refused naming Db: together they say the row is recorded and travels, rather than that the program was merely not refused.
